sources.citation: S.-J. Blakemore, D. M. Wolpert, C. D. Frith (1998). Central cancellation of self-produced tickle sensation. Nature Neuroscience.
sources.notes: Foundational UCL fMRI study (n=6) showing bilateral secondary somatosensory cortex and anterior cingulate suppression during self-generated vs externally produced tactile stimulation.

sources.citation: S.-J. Blakemore, C. D. Frith, D. M. Wolpert (1999). Spatio-temporal prediction modulates the perception of self-produced stimuli. Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience.
sources.notes: Robotic master-slave delay study (n=16) proving perceived ticklishness climbs monotonically across 0 ms, 100 ms, 200 ms, and 300 ms delays and across 0°, 45°, and 90° trajectory rotations.

sources.citation: S.-J. Blakemore, J. Smith, R. Steel, C. E. Johnstone, C. D. Frith (2000). The perception of self-produced sensory stimuli in patients with auditory hallucinations and passivity experiences: evidence for a breakdown in self-monitoring. Psychological Medicine.
sources.notes: Clinical study showing patients with passivity delusions fail to attenuate self-touch and can tickle themselves.

sources.citation: S.-J. Blakemore, D. M. Wolpert, C. D. Frith (2000). Why can't you tickle yourself? NeuroReport.
sources.notes: Synthesis of cerebellar internal forward models and efference-copy sensory attenuation.

sources.citation: K. Kilteni, H. H. Ehrsson (2020). Functional connectivity between the cerebellum and somatosensory areas implements the attenuation of self-generated touch. Journal of Neuroscience.
sources.notes: Modern 2020 human fMRI study proving cerebellum-to-S1/S2 functional connectivity directly mediates self-touch cancellation.

sources.citation: C. Press, P. Kok, H. Yon (2020). The perceptual paradox: how expectation sharpens and dampens sensory representations. Trends in Cognitive Sciences.
sources.notes: Modern predictive-processing critique reconciling initial sensory sharpening with post-surprise attenuation.
